issues.legal_issue: Rehabilitation authorities may revise and correct an allotment when later revenue records show that the land underlying it did not justify the full allotment, even without fraud, false representation, or concealment.
material_facts: The original allotment was based on an oral verification and was subject to correction if later revenue records justified it.
Later records obtained from the authorities in the country where the land had been left showed that some of the land was not canal-irrigated and that the allotment exceeded the entitlement.
A rehabilitation officer cancelled the excess, and the Chief Settlement Commissioner exercised revisional powers to cancel the allotment to that extent.

The beneficiaries argued that the absence of fraud, false representation, or concealment prevented revision and that the matter had been referred to the Chief Settlement Commissioner by an improper authority.
issues.conclusion: The rehabilitation officer had power to correct the allotment, and the Chief Settlement Commissioner could exercise the general revisional power notwithstanding the absence of fraud, false representation, or concealment. The referral for that exercise of power was not invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 19 and 24(1) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, an allotment could be corrected and the Chief Settlement Commissioner could examine the legality or propriety of an order and make an appropriate order. Section 24(2), which specifically addresses allotments obtained by fraud, false representation, or concealment, is illustrative and does not restrict the general power in Section 24(1). The Court relied on King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee, which held that a specific power stated without prejudice to general powers does not limit those general powers; it noted that Estate Development Ltd. v. Union of India did not decide this issue. The challenge based on Rule 102 and the asserted impropriety of the referral was rejected.

predicates.allotment_cancellation_appeal: A person appeals against an administrative decision cancelling some or all of a rehabilitation allotment.
predicates.provisional_allotment: The allotment was based on an initial verification that could be corrected in light of later information.
predicates.later_records_show_excess: Later records show that the land underlying the allotment did not support the full amount allotted.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges cancellation of an allotment initially based on provisional verification and later records show an excess, the rehabilitation authorities may correct the excess allotment.

issues.legal_issue: Verified revenue records showing the classification and irrigation of land may support a finding that an allotment exceeded the entitlement when no cogent contrary documentary evidence is produced.
material_facts: Records obtained from the relevant authorities were checked against original records and showed that the land included non-canal-irrigated categories as well as canal-irrigated land.
The authorities relied on the Fard Taqsim and Khasra Girdawari to determine the land’s classification and irrigation, and found that the allotment exceeded the entitlement.
The beneficiaries disputed the records’ reliability and argued that Jamabandi entries were preferable, but produced no cogent documentary evidence contradicting the records relied on.
The canal department entries sought by the beneficiaries had been destroyed or were unavailable; the revision authority left open the opportunity to produce cogent documentary proof later.
issues.conclusion: The authorities were entitled to rely on the Fard Taqsim and Khasra Girdawari, and the finding of excess allotment was upheld on the material available. The appeal was dismissed, without foreclosing the opportunity to seek correction on the basis of cogent contrary documentary proof.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the Fard Taqsim as an important revenue record capable of showing the extent, classification, and source of irrigation of land, and held that it could be relied on alongside the Khasra Girdawari. It referred to Sections 31–40 and Section 46 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, the relevant land-revenue rules and record forms, and the functions of Jamabandi, Khasra Girdawari, and Fard Taqsim. On the record before it, the authorities’ reliance on verified Fard Taqsim and Khasra Girdawari entries was justified; the beneficiaries could still seek correction by producing cogent documentary proof that the entries were wrong or the land was canal-irrigated.

rule.if: allotment_cancellation_appeal and official_revenue_records_verified and records_show_nonqualifying_land and no_cogent_contrary_proof

predicates.allotment_cancellation_appeal: A person appeals against cancellation of an allotment because the original allotment allegedly exceeded the entitlement.
predicates.official_revenue_records_verified: Officials check the relevant land records against original records and rely on them to assess the land.
predicates.records_show_nonqualifying_land: The records show that some of the land did not have the classification or irrigation characteristics supporting the full allotment.
predicates.no_cogent_contrary_proof: The person challenging the decision does not produce cogent documentary evidence contradicting the records relied on.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges cancellation of an allegedly excessive allotment, verified official records show land that does not support the full allotment, and no cogent contrary proof is produced, the cancellation is upheld.
